envelope.text: ADOPT-BOUNDED (RFC-0021): the wait DRIVES the context's executor — its

why: ADOPTED 2026-10-27 (phase-515 P5; maintainer decision the same day: spin while sleeping): `sleep_for(Duration rel_time, Context context)` (= `sleep_until(now() + rel_time, context)`) and the one-argument form; the `std::chrono` overload is not provided (phase-515 D1 keeps `<chrono>` interop declined). The refusal below was about a sleep that BLOCKS; this one does not -- the wait is one call into `nros_cpp_spin_until_clock`, which spins the context's executor (callbacks run during it) until THIS clock reaches the deadline, so a ROS-time clock driven by `/clock` wakes when simulated time arrives. The loop lives Rust-side, as `Rate::sleep`'s does in `nros_cpp_spin_for`, because a wrapper looping over `spin_once` is RFC-0020 class 2. ENVELOPE (stated on the declaration): callbacks run during the sleep, where upstream's sleep runs nothing; `false` without sleeping before `rclcpp::init`, for a deadline on another clock type (upstream throws), from inside a callback (not reentrant), or on a termination signal. Test: `packages/api/nros-cpp/tests/compile/clock_sleep_runtime.cpp`. PRIOR ROW: rclcpp's `Rate` blocks the calling thread in a sleep loop to hold a fixed frequency. RFC-0021 forbids a blocking helper that does not drive the executor -- a `Rate::sleep` on a single-threaded executor stops the transport for the whole period. The periodic work shape here is a timer, which the executor drives.
